To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the effects of micrometer size plastics on growth and lipid accumulation in microalgae are negligible in short-term tests and the polymer-size is the key factor influencing microplastic toxicity in microalgales.
the micrometer scale MPs did not influence the growth and lipid accumulation of the diatom, P. tricornutum but reduced algal inhibition by Phe.
the micrometer scale plastic particles (MPs) do not influence growth and lipid accumulation in microalgae under short-term (4 days) exposure.
In summary, our research is concerned with
microplastics in marine microalgae.
the effects of micrometer-scale plastic powders on microalgae and the role of plastic size on microplastic toxicity in microalgal cells.
the potential adverse effects of MPs on marine microalgaea and the key factors influencing the toxicity of MPs on marine algae.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
MPs do not have a significant effect on microalgae, especially in chronic tests.
the micrometer scale plastic pollution in the ocean would not have a significant negative impact on microalgae, which is the base of the marine food web.
the effects of micrometer size plastic on marine microalgal growth, phenanthren stress and lipid accumulation are not significant.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

microalgal growth and lipid content were not affected by micrometer scale plastics but the adsorption of MPs by microalgal cells could minimize the toxicity of organic contaminants in a combined MP and organic contaminant exposure system.
MPs in the hundred micrometer range would not be toxic to marine microalgae.
the size of MPs is the most critical parameter that should be considered when assessing the effects of MPs on marine microalgal growth and phenanthrene stress.
The main takeaway from our work is that
microalgae may be more tolerant to MPs in comparison to nanoplastics and that the adsorption of MPs is less influenced by size.
the polymer-size is the most important factor that should be taken into consideration in future laboratory experiments and eco-toxicologic assessments for microalgales.
the size of microplastics is a critical factor that should not be overlooked when conducting laboratory tests and assessing eco-toxicological risks for marine microalgae.
